info-theory-001.question: Let the amount of information obtained on being told that an event of probability p has occurred be −log₂ p bits. Which of the following is the amount of information obtained on being told that an event of probability 1/8 has occurred?
info-theory-001.explanation: The amount of information is −log₂(1/8) = log₂ 8 = 3 bits. Since 1/8 = 1/2³, it is the same amount of information as being told the answer to a "one of two" question of probability 1/2 three times over. The less likely an event, the more information we receive on being told that it has occurred.
choiceNotes: 0.125 is the probability 1/8 itself. The amount of information is not the probability but −log₂ p.
0.375 is −(1/8) × log₂(1/8) = 3/8, the term this event contributes when calculating the entropy. It is not the amount of information itself.
Correct. −log₂(1/8) = 3 bits.

info-theory-002.question: Which of the following correctly describes a property of the amount of information (−log₂ p on being told that an event of probability p has occurred)?
choices: The amount of information on being told that an event of probability 1, which always occurs, has occurred is 1 bit
The amount of information on being told that two independent events have both occurred is the sum of their individual amounts of information
The more probable an event, the more information we receive on being told that it has occurred
info-theory-002.explanation: Two independent events both occur with probability p₁ × p₂, so the amount of information is −log₂(p₁ × p₂) = (−log₂ p₁) + (−log₂ p₂), the sum of the individual amounts. Information is defined with a logarithm precisely to give it this additive property. Being told that a certain event has occurred tells us nothing new, so its amount of information is −log₂ 1 = 0.
choiceNotes: The amount of information of a certain event is −log₂ 1 = 0 bits. 1 bit is the amount of information of an event of probability 1/2.
Correct. Taking the logarithm turns the product of probabilities into a sum.
It is the other way round. The less likely an event, the more information we receive on being told that it has occurred.

info-theory-003.question: A source emits the symbols A, B, C and D independently with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8. Which of the following is the entropy (average amount of information per symbol) of this source?
info-theory-003.explanation: Entropy is the average of the amount of information −log₂ p of each symbol weighted by its probability: H = Σ(−p log₂ p). The symbols carry 1, 2, 3 and 3 bits of information, so H = 1/2 × 1 + 1/4 × 2 + 1/8 × 3 + 1/8 × 3 = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.375 = 1.75 bits. If the four symbols were equally likely it would be 2 bits, but a skewed distribution lowers it accordingly.
choiceNotes: 2 bits is log₂ 4, the value (the maximum) when the four symbols are equally likely.
2.25 bits is the plain average of the amounts of information 1, 2, 3 and 3, without weighting them by probability.

info-theory-004.question: Which of the following correctly pairs the maximum entropy of a source that emits 8 kinds of symbols with the condition under which it is reached?
choices: 3 bits; when one of the symbols has probability 1
3 bits; when all 8 symbols have probability 1/8
8 bits; when all 8 symbols have probability 1/8
info-theory-004.explanation: The entropy of a source emitting n kinds of symbols is greatest when every symbol occurs with the same probability 1/n, and its value is then log₂ n. For n = 8 this is log₂ 8 = 3 bits. The average information per symbol is greatest when the next symbol is hardest to predict. Conversely, when one symbol occurs with probability 1, we know what will come, so the entropy is 0.
choiceNotes: When one symbol occurs with probability 1, the entropy is at its minimum of 0 bits.
Correct. With equal probabilities it reaches the maximum of log₂ 8 = 3 bits.
8 is the number of kinds of symbols. The maximum entropy is its logarithm, log₂ 8 = 3 bits.

info-theory-005.question: A binary source emits 0 with probability 0.9 and 1 with probability 0.1, independently. Take log₂ 0.9 ≈ −0.152 and log₂ 0.1 ≈ −3.32. Which of the following is closest to the entropy of this source?
info-theory-005.explanation: H = −0.9 × log₂ 0.9 − 0.1 × log₂ 0.1 ≈ 0.9 × 0.152 + 0.1 × 3.32 ≈ 0.137 + 0.332 ≈ 0.47 bits. If 0 and 1 were equally likely it would be 1 bit, but here a 0 is almost predictable, so the average information per symbol is less than half of that. A skewed source like this can, with clever coding, be represented with fewer than 1 bit per symbol.
choiceNotes: About 0.14 is only the term for 0, −0.9 × log₂ 0.9; the term for 1 has not been added.
About 0.33 is only the term for 1, −0.1 × log₂ 0.1; the term for 0 has not been added.
Correct. Adding the two terms gives about 0.47 bits.

info-theory-006.question: A source that emits 8 kinds of symbols has an entropy of 2.4 bits. Defining redundancy as 1 − (entropy ÷ maximum entropy), which of the following is the redundancy of this source?
info-theory-006.explanation: The maximum entropy for 8 kinds of symbols is log₂ 8 = 3 bits, so the redundancy is 1 − 2.4 ÷ 3 = 1 − 0.8 = 0.2, that is, 20%. Redundancy expresses how much is wasted, because of skewed symbol probabilities and the like, compared with the maximum amount of information. The more redundant a source, the more room there is to shrink it with lossless compression.
choiceNotes: 25% is (3 − 2.4) ÷ 2.4, which divides the difference by the entropy instead of by the maximum entropy.
80% is 2.4 ÷ 3, the ratio of the entropy to the maximum entropy. Redundancy is 1 minus this ratio.

info-theory-007.question: For two random variables X and Y, which of the following correctly describes the conditional entropy H(X|Y) and the mutual information I(X;Y)?
choices: Knowing the value of Y can make H(X|Y), the uncertainty about X, larger than H(X) on average
The mutual information I(X;Y) is greatest when X and Y are independent, and its value is then H(X) + H(Y)
I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) is the reduction in uncertainty about X from knowing Y, and is 0 if they are independent
info-theory-007.explanation: H(X|Y) is the average uncertainty about X that remains after the value of Y is known; knowing Y never increases the average uncertainty, so H(X|Y) ≤ H(X). The reduction is the mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X, Y), and if X and Y are independent it is 0, because Y tells us nothing about X. In communication, with X the symbol sent and Y the symbol received, I(X;Y) is the amount of information actually conveyed per transmission.
choiceNotes: It does not increase on average. H(X|Y) ≤ H(X), with equality when X and Y are independent.
When they are independent, Y tells us nothing about X, so the mutual information is at its minimum of 0.
Correct. The reduction in uncertainty from knowing Y is the information Y gives about X.

info-theory-008.question: Two random variables X (value 0 or 1) and Y (value a, b or c) have the joint probabilities P(0, a) = P(0, b) = P(1, b) = P(1, c) = 1/4, and every other combination has probability 0. Which of the following is the mutual information I(X;Y)?
info-theory-008.explanation: X is 0 or 1 with probability 1/2 each, so H(X) = 1 bit; Y is a with 1/4, b with 1/2 and c with 1/4, so H(Y) = 1.5 bits. The four pairs each have probability 1/4, so H(X, Y) = 2 bits, and I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X, Y) = 1 + 1.5 − 2 = 0.5 bits. If Y is a or c the value of X is known, and if it is b it is not, so Y gives part of the information about X.
choiceNotes: Correct. 1 + 1.5 − 2 = 0.5 bits.
1 bit is H(Y|X) = H(X, Y) − H(X) = 2 − 1, the uncertainty about Y that remains once X is known.
1.5 bits is H(Y), the entropy of Y itself. It is not the part shared between X and Y.

info-theory-009.question: The 36 characters made up of the 26 capital letters and the 10 digits are to be distinguished by bit strings all of the same length (a fixed-length code). Which of the following is the minimum number of bits needed per character?
info-theory-009.explanation: n bits can distinguish 2ⁿ cases, so we need the smallest n with 2ⁿ ≥ 36. 2⁵ = 32 is not enough and 2⁶ = 64 is, so the answer is 6 bits. It is also log₂ 36 ≈ 5.17 rounded up to a whole number.
choiceNotes: 5 bits can distinguish only 2⁵ = 32 cases, too few for 36 characters.
Correct. 2⁶ = 64 ≥ 36.
36 bits is the case where each character gets its own bit and exactly one bit is 1 (one-hot), which is not the minimum.

info-theory-010.question: Which of the following correctly describes a variable-length code compared with a fixed-length code?
choices: It assigns codewords of the same length to every symbol, so there is no need to look for boundaries when decoding
It assigns shorter codewords to less probable symbols to shorten the average code length
It assigns shorter codewords to more probable symbols to shorten the average code length
info-theory-010.explanation: A variable-length code assigns short codewords to frequent symbols and long ones to rare symbols, shortening the average number of bits per symbol (the average code length). Morse code representing E, the most common letter in English, with a single dot follows the same idea. In exchange, the codewords are not all the same length, so the code is built to satisfy a condition such as being a prefix code, so that the boundaries can be determined in only one way.
choiceNotes: This describes a fixed-length code. A fixed-length code has fixed boundaries, but it cannot exploit skewed symbol probabilities.
It is the other way round. Making rare symbols short and frequent symbols long actually lengthens the average code length.
Correct. It exploits skewed probabilities to shorten the average code length.

info-theory-011.question: Which of the following sets of codewords assigned to four symbols is a prefix code (a code in which no codeword is the beginning of another codeword)?
info-theory-011.explanation: In a prefix code, a symbol is determined the moment its codeword has been read, so it can be decoded immediately without waiting for later bits (an instantaneous code). In {0, 10, 110, 111}, no codeword is the beginning of another. In {0, 01, 011, 111}, 0 is the beginning of 01 and 011, and in {00, 01, 1, 10}, 1 is the beginning of 10.
choiceNotes: 0 is the beginning of 01 and 011, and 01 is the beginning of 011, so it is not a prefix code.
Correct. No codeword is the beginning of another codeword.
1 is the beginning of 10, so it is not a prefix code. On receiving a 1, it is impossible to tell whether to cut there.

info-theory-012.question: A prefix code assigns the codewords A = 0, B = 10, C = 110 and D = 111 to the symbols A, B, C and D. Which of the following is the result of decoding the bit string 110100111 from the start?
info-theory-012.explanation: Read from the start and cut as soon as a codeword matches. 110 gives C, the following 10 gives B, 0 gives A and the remaining 111 gives D, so the result is CBAD. Because it is a prefix code, the string can be cut in only one way like this and can be decoded without any separator symbols.
choiceNotes: Encoding CABD gives 110, 0, 10, 111, that is, 110010111, which differs from the given bit string.
Encoding CBDA gives 110, 10, 111, 0, that is, 110101110, which differs from the given bit string.
Correct. It cuts into 110, 10, 0, 111.

info-theory-013.question: A binary prefix code is to be built by assigning codewords of the following lengths (numbers of bits) to the four symbols A to D. Which of the following sets of code lengths makes this possible?
info-theory-013.explanation: A prefix code with code lengths l₁, l₂, … can be built exactly when the Kraft inequality Σ 2^(−lᵢ) ≤ 1 holds. For 1, 2, 3, 3 the sum is 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8 = 1, so it can be built, for example as 0, 10, 110, 111. For 1, 2, 2, 3 the sum is 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/8 = 9/8, and for 1, 1, 2, 3 it is 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 = 11/8; both exceed 1, so neither can be built.
choiceNotes: Correct. The sum of 2^(−l) is exactly 1, and the code can be built as 0, 10, 110, 111.
The sum is 9/8, which exceeds 1. The length-1 word 0 and the length-2 words 10 and 11 use up every way a bit string can begin, leaving no room for a length-3 codeword.
The sum is 11/8, which exceeds 1. If both 0 and 1 are used as length-1 codewords, every other codeword must begin with one of them.

info-theory-014.question: A binary prefix code is being built, and the length-2 codewords 00 and 01 are already in use. Which of the following is the maximum number of length-3 codewords that can be added while keeping the prefix condition?
info-theory-014.explanation: There are 2³ = 8 bit strings of length 3, but the four that begin with 00 or 01 (000, 001, 010 and 011) cannot be used. The remaining four, 100, 101, 110 and 111, are not in a prefix relation with either 00 or 01, so all of them can be added. The Kraft inequality gives the same result: 2/4 + n/8 ≤ 1, so n ≤ 4.
choiceNotes: Correct. The four length-3 bit strings that begin with 1 can be used.
6 is the 8 length-3 bit strings minus the number of codewords used, 2. But 00 and 01 are each the beginning of two length-3 bit strings, so four cannot be used.
8 is every length-3 bit string, including those that begin with 00 or 01.

info-theory-015.question: A source emits the symbols A, B, C and D independently with probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1, and it is encoded with a Huffman code. Which of the following is the average code length per symbol?
info-theory-015.explanation: A Huffman code repeatedly merges the two smallest probabilities. 0.1 and 0.2 are merged into 0.3, then 0.3 and 0.3 into 0.6, and finally 0.6 and 0.4, so the code lengths are 1 bit for A, 2 bits for B and 3 bits for C and D. The average code length is 0.4 × 1 + 0.3 × 2 + 0.2 × 3 + 0.1 × 3 = 1.9 bits.
choiceNotes: About 1.85 bits is the entropy of this source, the lower bound of the average code length. The probabilities are not reciprocals of powers of 2 such as 1/2 or 1/4, so even a Huffman code cannot get that short.
2 bits is the code length of a fixed-length code that represents the four symbols with equal lengths.

info-theory-016.question: A source emits the symbols A to E independently with probabilities 0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.15 and 0.1, and it is encoded with a Huffman code. The codewords may change depending on which of two equal probabilities is chosen first, but the average code length does not. Which of the following is the average code length per symbol?
info-theory-016.explanation: First 0.1 and 0.15 are merged into 0.25, then 0.2 and 0.25 into 0.45, the remaining 0.25 and 0.3 into 0.55, and finally 0.45 and 0.55. The code lengths are 2 bits for A, B and C and 3 bits for D and E, and the average code length is (0.3 + 0.25 + 0.2) × 2 + (0.15 + 0.1) × 3 = 1.5 + 0.75 = 2.25 bits. For a source whose probabilities are not strongly skewed, a code with nearly equal lengths is shorter than one with stepped lengths such as 1, 2, 3, 4, 4.
choiceNotes: Correct. With code lengths 2, 2, 2, 3, 3 the average is 2.25 bits.
2.4 bits is the value when the code lengths are assigned in steps as 1, 2, 3, 4, 4. A prefix code can be built with them, but it is not optimal for these probabilities.
3 bits is the code length of a fixed-length code that represents the five symbols with equal lengths.

info-theory-017.question: A source emits the symbols A, B and C independently with probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1, and its entropy is about 1.30 bits. Which of the following is closest to the efficiency (entropy ÷ average code length) when this source is encoded with a Huffman code?
info-theory-017.explanation: The Huffman code merges 0.1 and 0.3 into 0.4 and then 0.4 and 0.6, so the code lengths are 1 bit for A and 2 bits for B and C. The average code length is 0.6 × 1 + 0.3 × 2 + 0.1 × 2 = 1.4 bits, and the efficiency is 1.30 ÷ 1.4 ≈ 0.93, that is, about 93%. The remaining 7% or so is waste that arises because code lengths are limited to whole numbers of bits.
choiceNotes: About 65% is 1.30 ÷ 2, the efficiency when the three symbols are represented with a 2-bit fixed-length code.
70% is 1.4 ÷ 2, the ratio of the average code length to that of the fixed-length code. It is not the efficiency.

info-theory-018.question: A binary source emits 0 with probability 0.8 and 1 with probability 0.2, independently. Symbols are taken two at a time, each of the four pairs 00, 01, 10 and 11 is treated as one symbol, and they are encoded with a Huffman code. Which of the following is the average code length per original symbol?
info-theory-018.explanation: The four pairs have probabilities 0.64 for 00, 0.16 for 01 and 10, and 0.04 for 11. 0.04 and 0.16 are merged into 0.2, 0.2 and 0.16 into 0.36, and finally that with 0.64, so the code lengths are 1, 2, 3 and 3 bits and the average per pair is 0.64 × 1 + 0.16 × 2 + 0.16 × 3 + 0.04 × 3 = 1.56 bits. Per original symbol this is 1.56 ÷ 2 = 0.78 bits. Coding one symbol at a time can only give 0 and 1 one bit each, but coding symbols together brings the length closer to the entropy of about 0.72 bits.
choiceNotes: About 0.72 bits is the entropy of this source, the lower bound of the average code length. Grouping only two symbols does not yet reach it.
Correct. 1.56 ÷ 2 = 0.78 bits.
1 bit is the value when the symbols are coded one at a time. Coding binary symbols one at a time needs one bit for each.

info-theory-019.question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between lossless compression and the entropy of a source?
choices: With a good enough lossless compression algorithm, any file, whatever its contents, can always be made smaller than the original
Even for a source that emits symbols independently, a cleverly designed lossless code can make the average code length smaller than the entropy
The average code length of a lossless code cannot be made smaller than the entropy, but coding symbols together brings it closer
info-theory-019.explanation: For a source that emits symbols independently, the average code length per symbol of a lossless code is at least the entropy, and coding symbols together brings it arbitrarily close to the entropy (the source coding theorem). Moreover, there are 2ⁿ files of n bits, but only 2ⁿ − 1 bit strings shorter than that in total, so no lossless compression can shorten every file. Lossless compression shortens data with skew or repetition at the cost of making other data slightly longer.
choiceNotes: By the pigeonhole principle, not every file can be shortened. Random data and data that are already compressed hardly shrink at all.
The entropy is the lower bound of the average code length. Trying to go below it produces a code that cannot be decoded in only one way.
Correct. The entropy sets the limit of lossless coding.

info-theory-020.question: The 40-character string AAAAAAAAAAAABBBBCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCDDDD (12 As, 4 Bs, 20 Cs and 4 Ds) is compressed with run-length encoding, which represents each run of the same character as a pair of "character (1 byte) and count (1 byte)". The original string uses 1 byte per character. Defining the compression ratio as "size after compression ÷ size before compression", which of the following is the compression ratio?
info-theory-020.explanation: There are four runs of the same character, A, B, C and D, so the compressed data are 4 × 2 = 8 bytes. The original is 40 bytes, so the compression ratio is 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2, that is, 20%. Run-length encoding shrinks data better the longer the same value continues.
choiceNotes: 10% is 4 ÷ 40, which leaves out the bytes that hold the count of each run.
Correct. 8 ÷ 40 = 20%.
80% is the fraction removed by compression (1 − 0.2), not the compression ratio as defined in this question.

info-theory-021.question: Which of the following data is most likely to be made smallest by run-length encoding?
choices: A drawing of black lines on a white background, represented as a two-level black-and-white image
An image such as a photograph, in which the values of neighboring pixels change finely
Data after encryption, in which 0s and 1s appear to be arranged at random
info-theory-021.explanation: Run-length encoding represents the length of a run of the same value as a number, so data in which the same value continues for a long time shrink the most. In a two-level drawing with a mostly white background, white pixels continue for long stretches, so the effect is large; fax coding also uses this idea. In data whose values change finely, the runs are short and the result can even be larger than the original.
choiceNotes: Correct. White and black pixels continue for long stretches, so there are few runs.
Pixels often differ from their neighbors, so the runs are short and the data hardly shrink, or even grow.
Data that look random contain almost no long runs of the same value and hardly shrink with any lossless compression.

info-theory-022.question: Which of the following correctly describes the idea of the LZ77 method used in ZIP, gzip and similar tools?
choices: It assigns short codewords to symbols with a high probability of occurring and long codewords to those with a low probability
It discards components that are hard for human eyes or ears to notice to make the data smaller
It replaces a string identical to one that appeared earlier with a pair of the distance back to that position and the length
info-theory-022.explanation: The LZ77 method uses the data already processed like a dictionary, and when the same string appears again it replaces it with a pair of distance and length, "so many characters back, for so many characters". It can shrink highly repetitive data without knowing the symbol probabilities in advance, and it is lossless compression that restores the original data exactly. The Deflate method of ZIP and gzip further encodes the output of LZ77 with Huffman codes.
choiceNotes: This is the idea of coding that uses symbol probabilities, such as Huffman coding.
This is the idea of lossy compression such as JPEG and MP3; LZ77 is lossless compression.
Correct. Repeated strings are represented by references to their earlier occurrences.

info-theory-023.question: Data compressed with the LZ77 method are to be restored. The data consist of "character A", "character B" and "(distance 2, length 5)", in that order. (distance d, length L) means repeating L times, one character at a time, "copy the character d characters back from the end of the restored string to its end". Which of the following is the restored string?
info-theory-023.explanation: Start from "AB", A followed by B. Copying the A two characters back gives "ABA", and then copying the B, now two characters back, gives "ABAB"; each copy moves the copy source forward by one, so copying five characters gives the seven-character "ABABABA". The length may thus exceed the distance, and by using just-copied characters as the source, a long repetition of a short pattern can be represented by a single pair.
choiceNotes: This treats only the two characters present at the start as the copy source. Since copying is done one character at a time, the copied characters also become sources for the next copies.
Correct. A, B, A, B, A are copied after AB, giving seven characters.
This copies the same A five times, but the end moves forward with each copied character, so the character two back alternates between A and B.

info-theory-024.question: When compressing data, which of the following must use lossless compression rather than lossy compression?
choices: Compressing a program's executable file for distribution
Shrinking video to match the speed of the connection in a video streaming service
Making music files smaller to listen to on a portable player
info-theory-024.explanation: Lossless compression restores the original data without a single bit of difference, while lossy compression discards parts that people hardly notice in return for much greater shrinkage. A program does not run correctly if even one bit differs, so lossless compression such as ZIP is used. Small differences in images and sound are hard to see or hear, so lossy compression such as JPEG, MP3 and video coding formats is widely used for them.
choiceNotes: Correct. An executable file does not run correctly unless it is exactly the same as the original.
Some degradation of video is acceptable, so lossy compression is used. On a slow connection, the picture quality is lowered to shrink it further.
Lossy compression such as MP3 and AAC is widely used. It shrinks files by discarding components the ear hardly notices.

info-theory-025.question: A single even parity bit is added to a bit string of data so that the number of 1s is even, and the receiver checks the number of 1s. Which of the following correctly describes this check?
choices: It detects a 1-bit error and also shows which bit is wrong, so the receiver can correct it
It detects an error when 2 bits are wrong at the same time, just as it does for a 1-bit error
It detects an odd number of bit errors but cannot detect an even number of bit errors
info-theory-025.explanation: If one bit flips, the parity (oddness or evenness) of the number of 1s changes, so the check reveals the error. If two bits flip, the parity returns to what it was, so the error goes unnoticed. In general, an odd number of errors is detected and an even number is not. Moreover, the check does not show which bit is wrong, so it cannot correct the error, and a response such as asking for retransmission is needed.
choiceNotes: It shows that there is an error, but not which bit. Correction needs a Hamming code or similar.
When two bits flip, the parity of the number of 1s returns to what it was, so the error is not detected.
Correct. The parity of the number of 1s changes only when an odd number of bits are wrong.

info-theory-026.question: Four rows of 4-bit data were sent with an even parity bit for each row at its right end and a final row of even parity bits for each column (vertical and horizontal parity). The received bits were row 1: 1011 1, row 2: 0100 0, row 3: 1100 0, row 4: 0101 0 and parity row: 0100 (the rightmost bit of each row is its row parity). If exactly one bit is wrong, which of the following is its position?
info-theory-026.explanation: Counting the 1s in each row, including the parity bit, gives 4 for row 1, 1 for row 2, 2 for row 3 and 2 for row 4, so only row 2 is odd. Counting the 1s in each column, including the parity row, gives 2 for column 1, 4 for column 2, 1 for column 3 and 2 for column 4, so only column 3 is odd. Therefore the bit where row 2 and column 3 cross is wrong, and flipping it corrects the error.
choiceNotes: Row 1 has four 1s, an even number, so row 1 contains no error.
Correct. Exactly one row and one column are odd, and the bit at their intersection is the wrong one.
This mixes up rows and columns. Row 3 has two 1s, an even number, so it contains no error.

info-theory-027.question: Data are added up one byte at a time, and the low 8 bits of the sum are sent along as a check value (checksum). Which of the following errors cannot be detected by this check?
choices: An error in which just one bit flips within one of the bytes
An error in which the value of one of the bytes becomes larger by 1
An error in which the order of two bytes is swapped
info-theory-027.explanation: Addition gives the same result in any order, so if two bytes are swapped the sum stays the same and the error cannot be detected. A single bit flip, or a change of 1 in the value of one byte, always changes the low 8 bits of the sum, so it is detected. With a CRC, the effect on the remainder of the division depends on the position of each bit, so in many cases such swaps are also detected.
choiceNotes: A single bit flip changes the sum by 2^k (k from 0 to 7), so the low 8 bits always change and the error is detected.
The sum changes by 1, so the low 8 bits change too and the error is detected.
Correct. Changing the order of addition leaves the sum the same, so the error is not detected.

info-theory-028.question: Three CRC check bits for the generator polynomial x³ + x + 1 (bit string 1011) are to be appended to the data 1101. The check bits are the remainder of dividing 1101000, the data followed by three 0s, by 1011, using exclusive OR instead of subtraction in the division. Which of the following are the check bits?
info-theory-028.explanation: Divide 1101000 by 1011. The exclusive OR of the leading 1101 and 1011 is 0110; bringing down the next bit gives 1100, whose exclusive OR with 1011 is 0111; 1110 with 1011 gives 0101; and finally 1010 with 1011 gives 0001, so the remainder is 001. The word sent is 1101001, and the receiver judges that there is no error if the remainder after dividing by 1011 is 0.
choiceNotes: Correct. The remainder of the division using exclusive OR is 001, and the codeword sent is 1101001.
101 is the remainder 5 obtained by dividing 1101000 and 1011 as ordinary binary numbers, 104 and 11. A CRC uses division by exclusive OR, without borrows.
110 is the remainder of dividing 1101 by 1011 without appending three 0s. The division is done after appending as many 0s as there are check bits.

info-theory-029.question: Which of the following correctly describes a CRC whose generator polynomial has degree r (r check bits) and a constant term of 1?
choices: For a 1-bit error, its main use is to identify which bit is wrong and correct it
It detects every burst error (an error confined to a contiguous range) of length r bits or less
With a well-chosen generator polynomial, it detects every possible error pattern
info-theory-029.explanation: Representing the error pattern as a polynomial E(x), a CRC fails to detect an error only when E(x) is divisible by the generator polynomial G(x). A burst error of length r or less can be written as x^i × B(x) (B(x) of degree r − 1 or less with a constant term of 1), which is not divisible by a degree-r G(x) with a constant term of 1, so it is always detected. On the other hand, patterns that are divisible, such as an error with the same form as G(x) itself, are not detected. CRCs are used mainly to detect errors, and when one is found the data are sent again.
choiceNotes: A CRC is used mainly to detect errors, and when one is found the data are sent again. Correction uses error-correcting codes such as Hamming codes.
Correct. A burst error of length r or less is not divisible by the generator polynomial, so it is always detected.
If the error pattern is divisible by the generator polynomial, the remainder does not change, so the error is not detected. Every generator polynomial has such patterns.

info-theory-030.question: Which of the following is the Hamming distance between the two 7-bit codewords 1011010 and 0110011?
info-theory-030.explanation: The Hamming distance is the number of positions at which the bits differ. The exclusive OR of the two words is 1101001, which has four 1s, so the Hamming distance is 4. Comparing bit by bit, bits 1, 2, 4 and 7 differ.
choiceNotes: 0 is the difference between the numbers of 1s in the two codewords (4 in each). The Hamming distance is counted by comparing bits position by position.
3 is the number of positions at which the bits agree.
Correct. The four positions at bits 1, 2, 4 and 7 differ.

info-theory-031.question: The minimum Hamming distance of a code (the smallest Hamming distance between any two codewords) is 5. Consider using it only for error detection, or only for error correction. Which of the following correctly pairs the number of bit errors that can always be detected with the number that can always be corrected?
choices: Detection up to 4 bits, correction up to 2 bits
Detection up to 5 bits, correction up to 2 bits
Detection up to 4 bits, correction up to 4 bits
info-theory-031.explanation: In a code with minimum Hamming distance d, an error of up to d − 1 bits never turns a codeword into another codeword, so it can be detected. Correction changes the received bit string to the nearest codeword, so if the number of errors is at most (d − 1) ÷ 2 rounded down, the original codeword remains the nearest. For d = 5, detection works up to 4 bits and correction up to 2 bits.
choiceNotes: Correct. Detection up to d − 1 = 4 bits and correction up to (5 − 1) ÷ 2 = 2 bits.
A 5-bit error can turn a codeword exactly into another codeword, in which case it is not detected.
With 3 or more bit errors, another codeword can be nearer than the original, and the word is corrected to the wrong codeword.

info-theory-032.question: Which of the following correctly pairs the minimum Hamming distance of the code consisting of the four codewords 00000, 01011, 10101 and 11110 with the number of bit errors it can always correct?
choices: Minimum Hamming distance 4; corrects up to 1 bit
Minimum Hamming distance 3; corrects up to 2 bits
Minimum Hamming distance 3; corrects up to 1 bit
info-theory-032.explanation: Of the six pairs, 00000 and 11110, and 01011 and 10101, are at Hamming distance 4, and the other four pairs are at distance 3, so the minimum Hamming distance is 3. It can correct up to (3 − 1) ÷ 2 = 1 bit. This code is a linear code, in which the exclusive OR of any two codewords is also a codeword, so the value 3 can also be found as the smallest number of 1s in a nonzero codeword.
choiceNotes: 4 is the largest distance. The number of errors that can be corrected is set by the distance between the two nearest codewords, that is, the minimum.
2 is d − 1, the value for detection only. Correction works only up to (d − 1) ÷ 2 rounded down.
Correct. The minimum Hamming distance is 3, so errors of up to 1 bit can be corrected.

info-theory-033.question: Which of the following is closest to the code rate of the Hamming (7, 4) code, which adds 3 check bits to 4 bits of data to form a 7-bit codeword?
info-theory-033.explanation: The code rate is k/n, the fraction of the codeword length n taken up by the k data bits. For the Hamming (7, 4) code it is 4/7 ≈ 0.57, so about 57% of the bits sent are data. A lower code rate means more check bits and makes it easier to resist errors, but lowers the efficiency of sending data.
choiceNotes: About 0.43 is 3/7, the fraction of the codeword taken up by check bits.
Correct. 4/7 ≈ 0.57.
1.75 is 7/4, with the numerator and denominator swapped. A code rate is 1 or less.

info-theory-034.question: In a Hamming (7, 4) code, the seven bits are numbered 1 to 7 from the left, and bits 1, 2 and 4 are check bits. They are set so that the number of 1s is even in bits 1, 3, 5 and 7 (check 1), in bits 2, 3, 6 and 7 (check 2) and in bits 4, 5, 6 and 7 (check 4). If the received word 0110001 has a single-bit error, which of the following is the wrong bit?
info-theory-034.explanation: In the received word 0110001, bits 1, 3, 5 and 7 are 0, 1, 0, 1, an even number of 1s (check 1 gives 0); bits 2, 3, 6 and 7 are 1, 1, 0, 1, odd (check 2 gives 1); and bits 4, 5, 6 and 7 are 0, 0, 0, 1, odd (check 4 gives 1). Reading the results of checks 4, 2 and 1 in that order, 110, as a binary number gives 6, so bit 6 is wrong. Flipping bit 6 gives 0110011, which satisfies all three checks.
choiceNotes: 2 is the position of bit 6 counted from the right. This question counts bit 1 from the left.
3 is the value of 011, the check results read in the order check 1, check 2, check 4. The check with weight 4 should be the most significant digit.
Correct. The check result 110 indicates the wrong position, 6.

info-theory-035.question: A SECDED code, which corrects 1-bit errors and detects 2-bit errors, is added to 32 bits of data. The number of check bits r of a Hamming code is the smallest value satisfying 2^r ≥ number of data bits + r + 1, and SECDED adds 1 bit of overall parity to this. Which of the following is the number of check bits needed?
info-theory-035.explanation: With r = 5, 2⁵ = 32 < 32 + 5 + 1 = 38, which is not enough, and with r = 6, 2⁶ = 64 ≥ 32 + 6 + 1 = 39, so the Hamming code needs 6 check bits. SECDED adds 1 bit of overall parity to distinguish 1-bit errors from 2-bit errors, giving 7 bits and a 39-bit codeword. For 64 bits of data the same calculation gives 8 bits, which yields the 72-bit width used for ECC in server memory.
choiceNotes: 6 bits is the number of check bits of a Hamming code that only corrects 1-bit errors. Detecting 2-bit errors needs one more bit of overall parity.
Correct. 6 + 1 = 7 bits.
8 bits is the number of check bits needed to add SECDED to 64 bits of data.

info-theory-036.question: Five Hamming (7, 4) codewords are lined up and sent in the order of bit 1 of each of the five codewords, then bit 2 of each, and so on (interleaving of depth 5). The receiver restores the original order and then corrects a 1-bit error in each codeword. Which of the following is the maximum length of a burst error, concentrated in consecutive bits, that can always be corrected?
info-theory-036.explanation: In the transmitted bit stream, bits of the same codeword appear every 5 bits. As a result, a burst error of 5 consecutive bits or fewer is split, after restoring the order, into at most one bit in each of the five codewords, and every one of them can be corrected by the Hamming code. With 6 bits, some codeword receives a 2-bit error and can no longer be corrected. Without interleaving, even a 2-bit burst error would fall into a single codeword.
choiceNotes: Correct. With a depth of 5, a burst error of up to 5 bits is split into one bit per codeword.
7 bits is the codeword length. A 6-bit burst error already puts a 2-bit error into some codeword.
35 bits is the total number of bits sent. Each codeword can correct only 1 bit, so a burst that long cannot be corrected.

info-theory-037.question: Which of the following correctly describes ARQ (automatic repeat request) and FEC (forward error correction), methods for dealing with errors in communication?
choices: ARQ corrects errors at the receiver alone, so no channel is needed to send notices back to the sender
FEC asks for retransmission when it detects an error, so delay tends to grow when there are many errors
FEC corrects errors at the receiver using redundant bits, so it can also be used for one-way broadcasting
info-theory-037.explanation: ARQ detects errors with a CRC or similar, tells the sender that the data could not be received and has them sent again; it needs a return channel and is delayed by the retransmissions. FEC sends redundant bits along with the data and corrects errors at the receiver alone, so it suits one-way broadcasting, communication with space probes where a round trip takes a long time, and communication that cannot tolerate delay. Real systems also often combine the two, correcting most errors with FEC and retransmitting the remaining ones with ARQ.
choiceNotes: This is a property of FEC. ARQ asks for retransmission, so it needs a channel from the receiver back to the sender.
This is a property of ARQ. FEC corrects errors at the receiver without asking for retransmission.
Correct. Errors can be corrected at the receiver alone, so it works without a return channel.

info-theory-038.question: In a binary symmetric channel, 0s and 1s are sent and each bit flips independently with probability 0.1. With the binary entropy function H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1 − p) log₂(1 − p), H(0.1) ≈ 0.469. Which of the following is closest to the channel capacity of this channel per transmission?
info-theory-038.explanation: The channel capacity of a binary symmetric channel is C = 1 − H(p), the value of the mutual information when 0 and 1 are sent with equal probability. For p = 0.1, C ≈ 1 − 0.469 = 0.531, about 0.53 bits per transmission. With suitable error-correcting codes, data can be sent at up to this rate with an arbitrarily small error rate. At p = 0.5, the received value is unrelated to the value sent, and the capacity is 0.
choiceNotes: About 0.47 bits is H(0.1), the uncertainty caused by the flips. The capacity is 1 minus this value.
Correct. 1 − H(0.1) ≈ 0.53 bits.
0.9 is the fraction of bits that arrive correctly, but the receiver does not know which bits flipped, so that information is lost and the capacity is smaller than 0.9.

info-theory-039.question: Which of the following correctly states Shannon's channel coding theorem?
choices: If the transmission rate is below the channel capacity, suitable coding can make the error rate arbitrarily small
With strong enough error-correcting codes, the error rate can be made arbitrarily small even at rates above the channel capacity
On a noisy channel, the only way to bring the error rate close to 0 is to bring the transmission rate close to 0 as well
info-theory-039.explanation: The channel coding theorem shows that at any rate below the channel capacity C, the error rate can be made arbitrarily small by using sufficiently long codes, and that this is impossible at rates above C. The theorem shows that such codes exist but does not give a concrete way to construct them. Today, codes whose performance approaches this limit (the Shannon limit), such as LDPC codes and polar codes, are in practical use.
choiceNotes: Correct. Below the channel capacity, codes exist that make errors arbitrarily rare.
At rates above the channel capacity, no code of any kind can make the error rate small.
With methods that simply repeat the same bits, errors do decrease only if the rate is lowered, but the theorem shows that errors can be reduced while keeping a fixed rate below the capacity.

info-theory-040.question: To convert a Gray code into an ordinary binary number, the most significant bit is used as it is, and each lower bit is found as the exclusive OR of the binary bit already found one position higher and the Gray code bit in the same position. Which of the following is the 4-bit Gray code 1101 converted into binary?
info-theory-040.explanation: The most significant bit is 1, the next is 1 ⊕ 1 = 0, the next 0 ⊕ 0 = 0 and the least significant 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, so the binary number is 1001 (decimal 9). As a check, the exclusive OR of 1001 and 0100, which is 1001 shifted right by 1 bit, is 1101, the original Gray code. In the Gray code, adjacent values differ in only one bit, as in 8 = 1100, 9 = 1101 and 10 = 1111.
choiceNotes: Correct. Finding 1, 1 ⊕ 1, 0 ⊕ 0 and 0 ⊕ 1 in turn gives 1001.
1011 is the result of applying the binary-to-Gray conversion (exclusive OR of adjacent bits) to 1101; the conversion goes the wrong way.
1101 is the value of the Gray code read as it is as a binary number.
